header: Date: 2026-04-16 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~49m | Redwood: Alex Chen (AE), Priya Desai (SE) | Arcadia: Jordan Miles (Lead ML Eng), Sofia Ramirez (Platform Eng), Tom Bennett (Head of AI)
summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on synthetic-session cohort experiments to improve overall KV/prefix cache hit rate. Reviewed current results (overall 22% hit rate with prefetch heuristics, high variance across cohorts), discussed cohorting strategy, TTL/eviction tuning, cache pollution from warmup spikes, and next steps: 48h synthetic bench, cohort TTL flags, and security demo request.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Alex from Redwood, Priya our SE, Jordan, Sofia, Tom from Arcadia. Uh, we'll run through the synthetic cohort results and then tune the TTLs and eviction policy.

[00:32] Jordan Miles: Thanks. Quick note — we saw some weird spikes in the first run, the warmup seemed to contaminate the cache, so before we dig in, just, like, heads up that the numbers vary a lot by cohort.

[01:05] Priya Desai: Yeah, that's expected; synthetic sessions help emulate cold-starts but can also produce high churn. We ran three cohort buckets: stable shoppers, promo-bounce users, and guest checkout. Summary: baseline (no prefetch) overall hit ~7%, with prefetch heuristics we got to ~22% overall, but stable shoppers hit as high as 38% and promo-bounce was only 9%.

[01:48] Tom Bennett: 38% — that's promising for the subset, but our worry is tail latency under warmup, right? If prefetch causes a lot of extra requests we might blow up token cost.

[02:10] Alex Chen: Good callout. In the bench we tracked per-token cost delta — prefetch increased compute by ~12% but reduced per-request latency p50 by 45ms and p95 by about 120ms for the stable cohort. Net savings depend on your traffic mix.

[03:02] Sofia Ramirez: Can you explain the implementation detail — are you prefetching full KV blocks or prefix-only? We've got limited KV capacity on dedicated instances.

[03:25] Priya Desai: Right now it's prefix prefetch plus hot KV entries (we treat KV as value-addressable frames). Implementation note: our prefetch heuristic uses session affinity + prefix frequency over a sliding 30m window. We added a protection: limit prefetch QPS to 20% of baseline to avoid flood.

[04:05] Jordan Miles: The cohort definitions — how are you assigning sessions to cohorts in synthetic runs? We want the mapping to mirror our real traffic (e.g., returning customers with saved carts).

[04:30] Priya Desai: For the synthetic bench we provided a mix generator. Cohort assignment uses three signals: cookie/session entropy, prior purchase flag, and time-since-last. We also test a randomized split to validate robustness. We'll share the generator config as a gist.

[05:12] Alex Chen: I just pasted the bench link in chat — bench CSV and config: https://redwood.internal/bench/arcadia-synth-0416 (note: demo link, access request needed).

[05:45] Tom Bennett: I got errors opening, might need permissions.

[06:00] Alex Chen: Yeah, I'll share a temporary S3 link after the call.

[06:20] Jordan Miles: Back to numbers — when you say prefetch increased compute 12%, is that GPU token cost or infra network? Need to map to our billing.

[06:45] Priya Desai: It's primarily GPU cycles — extra decoder steps for prefetch. Network egress was negligible because it's intra-node prefetch, but you'll see an uptick in token count reported in the bench. We can break that down per-cohort.

[07:30] Sofia Ramirez: Do you have an eviction policy suggestion? Our current TTL is static 10 minutes and we've been seeing churn with promo campaigns.

[07:50] Priya Desai: We're experimenting with an 'eviction thermostat' — dynamic TTL per cohort based on hit-rate momentum. If a cohort's hit-rate improves for N consecutive windows, TTL extends; if it drops, we cool down and shorten TTL to prevent cache pollution from ephemeral promos.

[08:30] Jordan Miles: That sounds useful, but how do you avoid oscillation? Campaigns come and go, so you might keep extending TTL for a short blip.

[08:55] Priya Desai: We use hysteresis: require 3 consecutive windows with >= 5% absolute improvement to extend and a backoff multiplier for TTL. Also we cap TTL per cohort to a max (e.g., 60m) to avoid forever caching.

[09:28] Tom Bennett: Any concern about state explosion if we have hundreds of micro-cohorts?

[09:45] Alex Chen: Good question. We store cohort metadata in a compact table; it's low-cardinality by design. For high-cardinality, we fall back to a hashed cohort with sampling. Cost remains small compared to KV store.

[10:10] Jordan Miles: What's the impact on warmup? We noticed that during batch loads the cache gets flooded and hit rate drops overall.

[10:38] Priya Desai: For warmup surge mitigation we added a prefetch ramp: limit concurrent prefetchers during initial ramp and prioritize stable cohorts. Also, we support synthetic session priming — run a short prefetch-only phase to warm targeted KV segments before traffic arrives. That's what we tested in the synthetic bench.

[11:20] Sofia Ramirez: We were considering synthetic priming weekly before Black Friday — could you simulate large promo spikes?

[11:42] Priya Desai: Yes, the bench supports spike events — you can inject promo cohorts with a burst profile. We ran a 2h spike test and saw temporary dip to 5% overall hit while stable cohort stayed above 30% because of priority routing.

[12:18] Jordan Miles: You mentioned route-by-policy earlier. Could we route high-value customers to dedicated capacity to ensure lower latency?

[12:40] Alex Chen: Absolutely — Redwood can route by tier: dedicated for top 5% customers, hosted for others. The tradeoff is cost. We can show a modeled cost/latency curve for different splits.

[13:05] Tom Bennett: Any security barriers for the synthetic bench? We need to ensure the bench doesn't leak PII when we run with our traces.

[13:25] Priya Desai: Standard process — you can anonymize the traces before upload. Also Redwood can run the bench inside your VPC/Private deployment if you prefer. For SOC2 concerns we can provide the SOC2 report and KMS integration doc.

[14:00] Sofia Ramirez: We'll probably want on-prem demo for the security team. Can we get that scheduled?

[14:12] Alex Chen: Yes, next_steps include an on-prem walkthrough. I'll coordinate dates with your security ops.

[14:45] Jordan Miles: Looking at the per-cohort CSV you linked earlier, I see a weird row — promo-bounce cohort shows negative hit delta after prefetch, is that a measurement bug?

[15:08] Priya Desai: That's likely measurement noise — if prefetch displaces high-utility items or exhausts capacity, local hit could drop. We'll re-run with stricter capacity caps.

[15:40] Tom Bennett: Also, please include tokenized prompt lengths — our prompts vary a lot across cohorts; prefix size matters.

[15:58] Priya Desai: Will do. We'll add column for median prompt token length and KV payload size.

[16:25] Alex Chen: Quick demo — Priya, can you share screen for the dashboard?

[16:38] Priya Desai: (screen share) Here's the per-route dashboard: p50/p95 latency, cost per 1k requests, per-cohort hit-rate sparkline. Notice the promo-bounce spike at minute 14 in the run, that's when synthetic promo traffic kicked in.

[17:20] Sofia Ramirez: The UI labels are slightly off — one says "KV hit" but it's actually prefix-hit, will that be fixed?

[17:35] Priya Desai: Good catch, labeling is sloppy in the dev dashboard. We'll push a fix.

[18:00] Jordan Miles: On instrumentation: can you surface token-level billing so we can map to our finance forecasts?

[18:20] Alex Chen: Yep, Redwood Console exposes token cost breakdown per-route and attributeable to cohort tags. We'll include a sample cost sheet.

[19:05] Tom Bennett: For the eviction thermostat, what's the safe default TTL and change policy we should try first?

[19:28] Priya Desai: Default we suggest: stable cohort TTL 30m, guest cohort 5m, promo cohort 3m; thermostat window 10m, hysteresis 3 windows. That got us to 22% overall in bench with less cache thrash.

[20:10] Jordan Miles: Can you quantify the burst protection? Like when a promo hits do we cap prefetch QPS to X?

[20:28] Priya Desai: In bench we used cap 20% of baseline QPS and concurrency cap of 50 prefetch workers. That prevented full cache saturation.

[21:00] Sofia Ramirez: Any thoughts on prefix coalescing? We have similar prefixes that differ only in tracking ids which fragment the cache.

[21:20] Priya Desai: Yes, we support prefix normalization rules — strip ephemeral tokens, canonicalize query order. We can add your rules to the bench. That usually increases hit by 3-10% depending on fragmentation.

[22:05] Jordan Miles: Great. One more thing — can we run bench against private deployment to validate on-prem latency?

[22:25] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Private can run the same bench inside your VPC. We'll need a short access window or run a containerized bench package. We'll include instructions.

[23:10] Tom Bennett: Our security team will ask for audit logs — do you capture cache-prefetch decisions and who triggered them?

[23:28] Priya Desai: We log prefetch decisions, cohort tags, TTL changes and make them viewable in audit logs. Retention is configurable per plan.

[24:05] Jordan Miles: Let's talk about success criteria for the pilot. We want at least 20% overall hit rate or 40% for stable cohort while keeping cost delta under 15%.

[24:30] Alex Chen: That seems reasonable and measurable. We can target those thresholds for the next run.

[25:05] Sofia Ramirez: Can you also report false-positive prefetches? Sometimes prefetch loads items never used in-session and that's wasted spend.

[25:28] Priya Desai: Yes, bench includes a prefetch utilization metric: percent of prefetched KV actually accessed later. We saw 72% utilization for stable cohort and 28% for promo in the current run.

[26:00] Jordan Miles: Ok, regarding data — Sofia will share anonymized session traces. About format, do you accept newline-delimited JSON?

[26:20] Sofia Ramirez: Yes, ndjson is fine, we'll scrub PII first.

[26:45] Alex Chen: Great. I'll put a checklist in the follow-up email.

[27:10] Tom Bennett: Any blocker on your side to run the 48h bench?

[27:22] Priya Desai: No blocker; just need the sample and confirmation of cohort weights. We'll start once we have the sample.

[28:00] Jordan Miles: A few quick clarifications — can you include the bench's random seed so results are reproducible?

[28:18] Priya Desai: Yes, every bench run logs seed and config. We'll include that in the CSV metadata.

[28:45] Sofia Ramirez: For the on-prem demo, our security team will want to see KMS/HSM integration and key rotation details.

[29:02] Alex Chen: We'll attach the KMS integration doc and SOC2.

[29:30] Priya Desai: Also, small note — we noticed a metric labeling bug that misreports prefix-hit vs kv-hit in the export. We'll fix and re-export the CSV.

[30:00] Jordan Miles: Is there any reason to test quantized model variants during the bench? We want to see latency differences too.

[30:20] Alex Chen: We can. Redwood supports model variants and quantization profiles. For bench comparatives we can run the same traffic across two model configs to compare token latency and output quality. Might add 12-24h to bench.

[31:05] Tom Bennett: Quality regression is a concern if we change models. Can you tie quality evals to the bench?

[31:25] Priya Desai: We can run differential evals on a held-out prompt set and report similarity metrics. We'll include basic ROUGE/BLEU-ish and human spot checks.

[32:00] Jordan Miles: Alright, let's capture action items — Alex, you'll run bench and share link; Priya will enable thermostat flags and add token length column; Sofia will upload traces.

[32:20] Alex Chen: Correct. I'll schedule the on-prem security walkthrough once Sofia confirms availability.

[32:45] Sofia Ramirez: We'll aim to have the sanitized traces by 2026-04-20.

[33:10] Priya Desai: One more operational note — if you want, we can add a 'dry-run' prefetch mode for production where prefetch decisions are logged but not executed; that helps estimate benefit without cost.

[33:30] Tom Bennett: That's exactly what we wanted — can you enable dry-run mode for one week?

[33:45] Priya Desai: Yes, we can flip that on.

[34:05] Jordan Miles: Cool. Any outstanding risks we haven't covered?

[34:20] Alex Chen: Risk: measurement noise and cohort mismatch. Mitigation: run multiple independent benches, use sample seed, and test on private deployment. Also watch for cost blowup if prefetch utilization is low.

[34:50] Sofia Ramirez: About utilization — is there a way to throttle prefetch more aggressively for promo cohorts?

[35:05] Priya Desai: Yep, cohort-level QPS caps are configurable.

[35:30] Tom Bennett: Ok that covers most. Let's do a quick recap and next steps.

[35:45] Alex Chen: Recap: Redwood runs 48h synthetic bench (50k sessions) with seed included; Priya enables cohort TTL/eviction thermostat and dry-run prefetch; Sofia uploads ndjson session traces; Alex to coordinate on-prem demo for week of 2026-04-27; we target success criteria: >=20% overall hit and <=15% cost delta.

[36:30] Jordan Miles: Sounds good. Thanks team.

[36:45] Priya Desai: I'll follow up with the updated CSV and corrected metric labels.

[37:10] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone, I'll send minutes and action items after the call.

[37:30] (end)

Notes: Transcript contains auto-generated timestamps and occasional mis-labels (e.g., KV vs prefix). Shared artifacts referenced: bench CSV link (access gated), sample config gist (to be shared), KMS/SOC2 docs to be attached in follow-up.
